name: UN Security Council Sanctions — Baseline Regimes
reference: UNSC Sanctions Regimes adopted under Chapter VII
supervisor: UN Security Council Sanctions Committees + Member States

chapters.title: Other UN regimes (1591 Sudan, 1533 DRC, 2140 Yemen, etc.)

articles.title: Authority — UN Charter Chapter VII
articles.requirement: UN Security Council determines a threat to international peace + security under Art. 39 and adopts measures under Art. 41 (sanctions, non-military) or Art. 42 (military). Sanctions resolutions are binding on all Member States under Art. 25. Each thematic / country regime is administered by a Sanctions Committee. Implementation is via national law; UN regimes form the floor for national + regional sanctions architecture.

articles.title: 1267 — ISIL/Al-Qaida asset freeze + travel ban + arms embargo
articles.requirement: Asset freeze on listed individuals + entities (ISIL (Da'esh) + Al-Qaida + associated individuals + entities). Travel ban. Arms embargo. List maintained by 1267/1989/2253 Sanctions Committee — typically 250-300 listings. Implementation by Member States through national designations (OFAC SDN + UK Consolidated + EU). Periodic review + de-listing mechanism through the Ombudsperson.

articles.title: 1718 — DPRK comprehensive regime
articles.requirement: Strict global sanctions: arms embargo (full); financial-services restrictions; designations (individuals + entities); prohibition on luxury goods exports; sectoral measures on coal + iron + ferrous metals + lead + seafood + textiles; restrictions on DPRK workers abroad; petroleum-products import caps. Detailed implementation guidance through the 1718 Committee Panel of Experts reports. Largest set of sectoral measures of any UN regime.

articles.title: 2231 — Iran (JCPOA framework)
articles.requirement: Endorses the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (14 July 2015). Lifts certain UN sanctions on Iran subject to the snap-back mechanism (Annex B). Maintains restrictions on certain nuclear-related items + designated individuals + entities. The snap-back mechanism allows a JCPOA participant to trigger re-imposition of pre-2015 UN sanctions in 30 days. Iran-related UN measures continue to interact with US (broader, including secondary) + EU + UK sanctions architectures.

articles.title: Other UN regimes (Sudan / DRC / Yemen / Libya / Mali / CAR / Haiti / Somalia)
articles.requirement: Other active UN regimes: Sudan (UNSCR 1591); DRC (UNSCR 1533); Libya (UNSCR 1970 + 2011); Mali (UNSCR 2374 + 2723); CAR (UNSCR 2127); Yemen (UNSCR 2140); Somalia (UNSCR 751 + 1907); ISIL/Al-Qaida (UNSCR 1267); Haiti (UNSCR 2653). Each regime has its own Sanctions Committee + Panel of Experts + listing criteria. National implementation follows the same pattern as for 1267 / 1718 / 2231.

articles.title: Member State implementation
articles.section: UN Charter Art. 25 + Member State law
articles.requirement: All UN Member States are bound to implement UN sanctions under Art. 25 of the UN Charter. Implementation modalities: (a) national designation legislation reflecting UN listings (US — OFAC; UK — OFSI; EU — Council Reg incorporating UN list); (b) trade controls per UN sectoral measures; (c) reporting + cooperation with the Sanctions Committee; (d) implementation reports to the Sanctions Committee (annually or as requested).

articles.title: National layer-ons (autonomous sanctions)
articles.requirement: UN regimes form the floor; national + regional sanctions architectures layer additional autonomous measures (US OFAC autonomous programs; UK SAMLA regimes; EU CFSP autonomous regimes). Compliance requires screening against the UN-baseline + the more expansive national layers. Where the layers conflict (e.g. UN sanctions lifted but national sanctions remain), national sanctions prevail for that jurisdiction's persons.

articles.title: Listing review + de-listing mechanisms
articles.requirement: UN listings are reviewed periodically by the responsible Sanctions Committee. The 1267 Ombudsperson handles independent de-listing petitions for the ISIL/Al-Qaida regime (the only UN regime with an Ombudsperson). For other regimes, de-listing requires consensus in the relevant Sanctions Committee. Court challenge available in some Member States (e.g. CJEU Kadi line of cases) on procedural due process.
